WHO_BASE = "https://ghoapi.azureedge.net/api/"

def fetch_who_indicator(indicator_code, spatial_type="COUNTRY"):
    """Fetch all country-level data for a WHO GHO indicator."""
    url = f"{WHO_BASE}{indicator_code}"
    params = {"$filter": f"SpatialDimType eq '{spatial_type}'"}
    
    all_records = []
    while url:
        resp = requests.get(url, params=params)
        resp.raise_for_status()
        data = resp.json()
        all_records.extend(data.get("value", []))
        url = data.get("@odata.nextLink", None)
        params = {}  # nextLink already has params
    
    df = pd.DataFrame(all_records)
    return df

    d = df.copy()
    if has_sex and "Dim1" in d.columns:

    d = d[["SpatialDim", "ParentLocationCode", "ParentLocation", "TimeDim", "NumericValue"]].copy()

        "SpatialDim": "country_code",
        "ParentLocationCode": "who_region_code",
        "ParentLocation": "who_region",
        "TimeDim": "year",
        "NumericValue": value_col_name
    })
    d["year"] = d["year"].astype(int)
    return d

WB_BASE = "https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/all/indicator/"

def fetch_wb_indicator(indicator_code, start_year=2000, end_year=2024):
    """Fetch World Bank indicator for all countries."""
    all_records = []
    page = 1
    while True:
        params = {
            "format": "json",
            "date": f"{start_year}:{end_year}",
            "per_page": 1000,
            "page": page
        }
        resp = requests.get(f"{WB_BASE}{indicator_code}", params=params)
        resp.raise_for_status()
        data = resp.json()
        
        if len(data) < 2 or not data[1]:
            break
        all_records.extend(data[1])
        
        total_pages = data[0]["pages"]
        if page >= total_pages:
            break
        page += 1
    
    rows = []
    for r in all_records:
        if r["value"] is not None:
            rows.append({
                "country_code": r["countryiso3code"],
                "country_name": r["country"]["value"],
                "year": int(r["date"]),
                "value": float(r["value"])
            })
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

title: Infectious vs. Non-Communicable Disease Burden Across Regions and Income Levels
text:
Research Questions

How do infectious versus non-communicable disease patterns differ across WHO regions and World Bank income groups?
Which country-level factors — GDP, health spending, urbanization — best explain that variation?

title: Infectious vs. Non-Communicable Disease Burden Across Regions and Income Levels
text:
Key Findings

Low-income countries face a “double burden” — they carry the highest rates of both infectious diseases (TB, HIV, malaria) and non-communicable diseases simultaneously, challenging the simple epidemiological transition model.
Disease burden strongly predicts economic status. An XGBoost classifier can accurately distinguish income groups using only health and economic indicators, with low-income countries being the most distinctly identifiable.
Life expectancy is highly predictable from disease and economic indicators. The composite infectious disease burden score and malaria death rate are the most powerful predictors, more so than GDP or health spending alone.
Progress is real but uneven. All income groups have seen improvements from 2000 to 2021, but the gap between low- and high-income countries persists, and COVID-19 caused a visible setback in 2020.
How much a country spends on health matters less than what it spends on. Health expenditure as a share of GDP shows surprisingly weak association with actual health outcomes, suggesting that resource allocation is more important than total spending.

Figure 2: Sunburst Chart — Disease Burden Hierarchy
This sunburst chart reveals the hierarchical structure of global TB burden: the inner ring shows WHO regions, the middle ring breaks each region into World Bank income groups, and the outer ring shows individual countries. Sector size encodes the mean TB incidence (per 100,000), and color encodes life expectancy — darker purple indicates lower life expectancy, brighter yellow indicates higher. Click any sector to drill down into that region or income group; click the center to zoom back out. The chart makes immediately visible that the Africa region dominates global TB burden, and that within Africa, low-income countries carry the heaviest load with the lowest life expectancy.

text:
1.4 Hyperparameter Tuning (RandomizedSearchCV)
XGBoost minimizes a regularized objective with L2 (\(\lambda\)), L1 (\(\alpha\)), and tree complexity (\(\gamma\)) penalties:
\[
\mathcal{L} = \sum_i \ell(y_i, \hat{y}_i) + \sum_k \left[ \gamma T_k + \frac{1}{2}\lambda \lVert w_k \rVert^2 + \alpha \lVert w_k \rVert_1 \right]
\]


Code
param_dist_clf = {
    "max_depth": [3, 5, 7, 9],
    "learning_rate": [0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.3],
    "reg_lambda": [0.1, 1, 10],
    "reg_alpha": [0, 0.1, 1],
    "subsample": [0.7, 0.8, 1.0],
}

rand_search_clf = RandomizedSearchCV(
    estimator=XGBClassifier(
        n_estimators=300, eval_metric="mlogloss",
        importance_type="gain", random_state=42, n_jobs=-1
    ),
    param_distributions=param_dist_clf,
    n_iter=30,
    cv=StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=42),
    scoring="f1_macro",
    random_state=42, n_jobs=-1, verbose=1
)
rand_search_clf.fit(X_train_c, y_train_c)

print(f"Best params: {rand_search_clf.best_params_}")
print(f"Best CV Macro F1: {rand_search_clf.best_score_:.3f}")
